full_text:
Interviewer:	I'll tell you a bit about what I'm doing – we're looking at women students, mainly engineering students. We're also doing the work in another university, and the design and technology side comes under engineering there, so we've included it here as well.  The main thing we're looking at is the fact that engineering's male dominated, so it will be interesting to get your views on that side of thing as well. So we're really trying to improve the situation for women in engineering. Erm, are you going on a placement?

Subject:	I'm not sure, I've applied to [company] so far and some others I've looked at, but erm, I'm actually living in [university town] next year, so whatever I get, you know, I want to be in travelling distance – so I'm going to apply for a few places, but if not, then I'll just carry on to the third year.

Interviewer:	We'll start off with a few background questions about why you chose the course. OK, what is the course exactly?

Subject:	Industrial design and technology.

Interviewer:	What A levels did you do?

Subject:	I did Art, English Literature, Design and Technology and then I did general studies. I also did an AS in Biology, but dropped that – it wasn't really for me.

Interviewer:	What type of school did you go to?

Subject:	Er, just a normal, basic school.

Interviewer:	Yes, not an all girls school or anything like that?

Subject:	Oh no.

Interviewer:	Erm, have you got any previous work experience in the industry?

Subject:	No, no none at all, no.

Interviewer:	Ok, what do your parents do – are either of them engineers?

Subject:	My dad's an engineer – well, that's what course he did – he's a Project Manager, and my mum just works part time.

Interviewer:	OK, when and why then do you think that you decided to do design and technology?

Subject:	Well, I'd already been interested – well through school, I'd always been interested in Art and I'd always wanted to do something with that and then I got to college and I did design and technology and I did really enjoy that as well and I thought doing the technology will be using my brain more than the arts – you know people always say oh I can't get a job in a art, so I thought oh, I'll take that course then. And I do still enjoy you know, some arty aspects, and I do try and get – you know – sort of that into my work. Yeah, I decided – I was either going to be a graphic designer or it was just, you know, design technology and talking to my tutors and everything and they said, oh well maybe you should go for the design technology then it's a bit – it's not – it's still a bit creative but you can use your brain in other aspects of the stuff rather than going for a tot – you know graphic design – it's hard to get a job in those sort of areas. So then I decided on industrial design in the end. I didn't quite realise how much technology would be involved though, 'cos like on the open day they said – I said, oh well I did Maths at GCSE, and I got an A for that, and so will I be OK? And they said, oh yeah, if you get the C at GCSE you're fine and I got here and it was really difficult, I found it really hard. And a lot of people did. I think a few of the people did drop out in the first year because, it didn't seem to be specified that – you know actually that you'd be having electronics every week and then you swap over and do mechanics and you'll have tests on these and then. Yeah, I did Ok on some of the mechanics stuff, 'cos I didn't – well, they teach you, you know – taught that quite well, but some of the electronics I did really struggle on that, so it did sort of put me off the course but then I thought I'll stick with it and see, you know, if it gets easier and obviously this year I didn't have to take that – I chose, you know, other aspects that I preferred so…

Interviewer:	OK, did you have much advice and that, from careers advisors, then?

Subject:	Erm, I didn't really at secondary school. I didn't really – they never said that much, to be honest, but I sort of always had in my mind, that I knew which sort of course I wanted to do and so it was just a matter of deciding whether it was going to be graphics or design technology, so, you know.

Interviewer:	Did your family influence your decision at all?

Subject:	Yeah, they did sort of because my Mum did say well, maybe you should do industrial design, instead of graphic design because it's – you know – quite difficult to get a job in graphics design. Yet with something like industrial design, because there's a lot of different areas you can go into then, they said you're probably better to do that.

Interviewer:	OK, did you think about doing the sandwich course when you applied for the course?

Subject:	Yeah, when I applied for the course they said oh, you can put down the sandwich course anyway, even if you decide not to do it. So I thought well I'll put down for it, because you know, a lot of people say that obviously it'll help you in your job if you've had some work experience, because nowadays that's what they look for. Rather than oh, you've got this grade, or whatever, it's what experience you've got so I thought it'd be valuable to put that down…

Interviewer:	OK, how did you decide to come to [this university]?

Subject:	Erm, well that was – I put down – I had loads of universities and I thought, oh I don't know which one to go to, went all over the country like going to student days there, just thought seeing like the feel about the place, what I preferred and it came down to either [university] or here and – because my tutor said, oh, have you looked at [this university]? 'Cos I hadn't – I'd never really heard of it and he said, oh 'cos it's really good for design and technology and everything. So I came here and I thought, oh yeah, it does seem really good and it's like an academic sort of university and everything. So I thought oh yeah – I decided to come here in the end. But I was very umming and ahhing like till the last minute.

Interviewer:	Ok, is design and technology very male dominated?

Subject:	Well, yeah, there isn't very many females on the course. Obviously its increasing all the time but I do find that, obviously, in the first year, with all the electronics and mechanics, there's – the guys can think it – you know, with different parts of their brain to like –apply it to that sort of thing whereas I think – some girls are really good at it as well – you know – it's quite, you know, a hard thing to get it – you know – to take that on board.

Interviewer:	What characteristics do you think make a good designer and do you think any of those characteristics are more male or female?

Subject:	Erm, I suppose the – well there is like an Arty sort of side, you know, the sort of creative side, which is a lot of – erm, it did surprise me actually, because a lot of the males are very good at that as well, whereas at secondary school it's always been more the female sort of side, whereas men do more – do making and things. And also, we have projects where we had to make like prototypes – just models and stuff – and I found that quite difficult because I'd never done it before, whereas the boys, they, even though they've not done as much they seem to have like a better understanding of how to do it. Like, they got told, then they could apply it straight away – whereas I had to ask them again and again how to do it – I just couldn't get my head around them.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that more women should be encouraged to do design and technology?

Subject:	Yeah, I think it is good that you know – to encourage more people to do it, if it's – well, it's a good course, you know, and very varied so.

Interviewer:	Why do you think that more women don't do it – do you think that's because they don't know what it is?

Subject:	Yeah, maybe. I'd have thought, because I applied to like loads of different places for like design and technology and then, here, it was the industrial design, but I sort of thought that was the same as design and technology, so I looked at it, you know, and looked at loads of different universities and I realise now that the industrial design is obviously more technical than say the course at [university] which was design technology. So yeah, I suppose people don't really understand it totally and I can't remember in the prospectus, whether it actually said I would be doing electronics and mechanics. I think all I thought as well would be oh you'd be doing like ergonomics, and sizes and – which I did really enjoy that part and then, obviously, aesthetics and everything. I didn't know if it said – you know – about those or not.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think could be done to let people know more about it. Do you think that's down to – purely down to school or…?

Subject:	I think it's probably – yeah, through careers advice or you know, because I'm sure people kind of think oh, I won't be able to do that, because it's got this in it or its all male dominated, but I think sort of now, it does seem to be – more people do seem to be interested in doing these, you know, all these sort of careers. I think it's like – because in hall last year, we had a few engineering students and some of those were girls and they did seem to get on OK on the course and obviously you think sometimes oh that's quite odd that they're doing it but, so, my dad did – because he'd worked in engineering, he said that they're always looking for like – now – they've got like 1 female engineer and he said that she's really thorough, because obviously, it depends whether - the guys tend to be 'oh yeah, I'll just do it like that' or whether there's quite – he said that she's really good, so. I suppose they should be encouraged to say oh look, you can do it.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there are any advantages to being a woman in a male dominated …?

Subject:	Yeah, I think so because er – especially when we've done like er group work or things like that. We have different perspectives than the males. I think also – I also, personally, I try to see things a bit differently as well, because I enjoy not the technical side, I'll look into more arty stuff and there are different ways to do stuff. And I think it is much more interesting having, like a broad range of people, come up with such different ideas.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there are disadvantages?

Subject:	Erm, I suppose a disadvantage – er, I feel that I'm not quite as technology er minded as some of the guys are.

Interviewer:	OK, I'm going to ask you a few questions about the course and that now. You've said a bit about the course not being exactly what you expected it to be (yeah) but what do you think have been the best and the worst things about the course so far?

Subject:	Er, the best thing is – I enjoy working within – I do quite like working in the group work like, I very much like brain storming, you know, at the beginning of a project and stuff like in a small group or er we've done presentations and things as well. At first I thought, oh no, I hate doing them but it does get you much more used to it, ready for – say in design – we had part of that, the assessment was to do presentations – so that was really good. And then, also erm just sort of other presentation boards and sketching's quite good. I don't always like it when you have to – say when the specification – like's so rigid, and they say do this and you have like, you know, follow it totally. I like it when – like we've recently had this project on – it was researching into different topics for (?) and I had waking up and going to sleep. It's also about – really interesting like asking people all what do you like? What do you hate? And taking like – recording it and photos as well and then we created a board to do that. Like you can see that obviously all the different presentation boards were totally different, because obviously how things are perceived is different. But I did really enjoy doing that because you can put much more of your influence into it rather than saying oh, do a ¾ perspective of this product. There are also things that I don't like, sort of electronics. I'm not keen on the CAD – you know – computer aided design. I just find it really difficult. I just – to get my head round it, I just like – I think it makes it a challenge – I haven't done it before and – I mean I do – I can do stuff – you know some stuff now, which I couldn't do before but I still struggle a bit and initially – when I get an assignment of it, I'm like oh no. 

Interviewer:	Do you think then, like you said you like doing the group work and presentations and stuff – do you think that'll help you when you go to work?

Subject:	Yeah, definitely, yeah. I think the group work's really good, so erm, understand like how to deal with anyone that thinks differently and yet trying to get all that group together to come up with a solution and things. And, obviously, the presentations erm although sometimes you might dread them, they are really useful because you'll have to do that anyway, whatever job you go into really. So it's confidence and things.

Interviewer:	When you do group work, how do you decide who to work with, in your groups?

Subject:	Erm, sometimes we get set them, which is quite good I suppose, because then you can have a mix of different people you haven't worked with and you can get to know other people – what they think about. Or, recently, at the moment, we're just in a group and we pick that ourselves, so usually just friends or whatever. I don't usually go for like well, I'll go with them, they're really good at things. I just usually go with friends and then I know that we'll get on and we'll be able to motivate each other and such like.

Interviewer:	Do you prefer to work with men or women or doesn't it bother you?

Subject:	Er, I don't mind to be honest – either. I think it's good to have a mixture, really. And on our course you always do because there's hardly any females – there all dotted about, but there's more – you know – more males.

Interviewer:	Have you had any really bad experiences with group work at all?

Subject:	Erm, I haven't really, to be honest. I know sometimes it's hard – like, if there's one person who's not pulling their weight, but I've never really had that, so it's been OK, you know so far.

Interviewer:	Out of interest, what are the gender proportions?

Subject:	I think there are probably about – I'm trying to think how many females there are. Maybe about – I'd say maybe about a quarter female and the rest male. Something about that.

Interviewer:	Is that the same with lecturers as well – do you have any female lecturers at all?

Subject:	Erm, the only – we used to have – well, we had – one of our Heads of year, she was called [name], but she left and we had a – but mostly they're all males, to be honest. I don't think they have any – we have one lady actually for sustainable, but yeah, they're generally male, you know for the CAD and then – I think it would be quite good having a female actually, teaching from a (?) then you probably get a better perspective on it, because obviously the males are like – they explain it in a different way, which is sometimes hard to follow.

Interviewer:	Do you think it would be quite encouraging having a female?

Subject:	I think it would, yeah, because then you'd think oh well, look how well they're doing – I'll try and you know, apply for that. Yeah, I never thought about that before but I think that would be quite good.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the male lecturers treat the female and male students the same?

Subject:	Er I think sometimes they make like – I find that sometimes, within technology sort of thing, you'll ask them a question and they'll tell you, then you still haven't got it and then they sort of think – 'what do you mean, you don't understand?' And sometimes I think you don't get – they don't think it'll help. But then, if you say, oh we're only here to lecture, we're not here to teach, but it is quite difficult when you do ask, they sort of explain it and then you're like well, I still don't get that. And I often have to ask males in the group and then they'll explain it and I'm like, oh right, that's what he's going on about, I know now - so yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, have you got a personal tutor?

Subject:	Er, yeah.

Interviewer:	Are they male or female?

Subject:	Male, yeah.

Interviewer:	Would you rather have a female for your tutor?

Subject:	Erm, I think there's one – I think there's one lady – female – I think all the rest are male, so…

Interviewer:	Would you rather have a female?

Subject:	Yeah, I think it would be good, actually, to have a female, yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think they'd be more approachable?

Subject:	Yeah, I do find that our tutors aren't very approachable and I find with [name] – well she's very approachable, you can ask her about anything, I'd feel comfortable asking her, you know, about your problems or anything, but I do find some of the others like – I wouldn't ever want to go and say, oh, what do you mean about this but I feel like they think I'm stupid or oh what do you mean do you didn't know it? Because I do often get that impression so…

Interviewer:	Do you think that that's a bit as well, because you are a woman?

Subject:	Yeah, it could be maybe yeah, although some like – we do have someone in for electronics and he's male and obviously he helps the females more and so the guys get annoyed about that and he's alright to help you. He's like oh let me help you with that circuit and then the guys will come up to him and ask him and he's like oh well, oh you do it like this but then sends them all off – so that's quite good – using it to your advantage.

Interviewer:	What bits of the teaching and advice that you've had might help you when you get on placement?

Subject:	I don't really think – feel that anything would, to be honest. I don't – I mean the teaching it's more – I think you have to do it more off your own back, to be honest, because you – as we said – they just lecture, they don't really – they're not bothered about if you – really, you know, you can understand it really, because they're just there to tell you about all the facts and then you have to apply it yourself and advice I haven't really – I meant I don't ever really go and talk to my personal tutor because I don't find that, you know, it'd be that beneficial really. So…

Interviewer:	Do you think that there are any skills that you've learnt, on the course, that will help you?

Subject:	Well, I think, well I've gained more confidence, obviously through the group work and getting on with other people, and presentations. I mean I must say – you could say like working to deadlines, but I still leave things to the last minute – I always plan to do them, you know, but it never happens. And I've been finding a lot of people on the course are – do seem very organised and I wish they could like, you know, rub some of that off onto me. I could do with some of that.

Interviewer:	OK, do you feel ready to go on placement?

Subject:	No, I don't, no. And I think that's why I sort of, you know, holding back a bit not totally – like a lot of people that have applied to all them places and have got – some people have got accepted already. But I sort of – you know, left it till the last minute. I've applied to [company] but I looked at some others on the internet but I'm just sort of like thinking, oh God, I don't think I can do these things, like it looks very like you've got to be efficient in CAD and stuff and I'm like well, I'm not really that, you know. I don't feel that I could be you know, be out in the workplace, if someone was telling me to do something, I'd be like, oh God, you know. But also, I've looked at some placements which are quite different, so I do like – in my freetime, I like making like bags and clothes and stuff, so I've sort of looked into some stuff like that. So I might apply to some of those – like more craft sort of things rather than in technology sort of things.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the university could do more to help prepare you?

Subject:	Yeah, I think there would be a lot – it's like just to help you get – I mean we had help with CVs and you know, how to approach – your work and stuff together, but yeah it would be handy to like have something, even if it's partly like the tutors would say, you know, we're going to have a meeting with every one of you and talk to you about how – you know – and what you want to do and stuff – I think that would be quite useful.

Interviewer:	Have you had the chance to speak to anyone like that's been on the course before and maybe been on a placement?

Subject:	Yeah, that'd be quite useful, yeah.

Interviewer:	What do you think will be the good things about going on placement?

Subject:	Er, money (laughs). It'll be good to like, because obviously – I don't think the company that I plan to work for (?). I think it will be good to like have a different sort of outlook on the course, 'cos I do find like and I do often go through stages and I'm like Oh God, I'm not sure if I'm on the right course. I should have done like English or something – because, you know, to have more time for fun stuff rather than like always – 'cos this course is like really demanding and it's always – you're always thinking about it, you've always got a deadline, and it just seems like really stressful whereas, in my house, like there's other people who are doing like other courses and who don't have much to do, yet they'll get better grades at the end of the day.

Interviewer:	Do you think it's seems strange that you're in the social sciences and humanities faculty?

Subject:	Yes, it does seem quite odd, yeah, yeah. 

Interviewer:	When you've been looking at the companies –have you been looking at the type of work that you'll be doing or have you been looking at things like training opportunities and the pay and things like that?

Subject:	Erm, just sort of looking at the – what you'd have to do really, and what sort of skills they want so you know, I can see whether I'd be suitable for it or not. Because, obviously they're not that detailed in, you know, the description – I mean you might be OK, some of the work so they do obviously get – it's the way they've worded it, you're like Oh no, I wouldn't be able to do any of that.

Interviewer:	OK, have you done much research on the different companies then?

Subject:	I just – well the only place I've looked is on the –you know – [university] – careers website – I've just looked at industrial placements on there. But a lot are very technical which I obviously don't want, so I sort of looked in the – like you can go on the database and I was like crafts for – and it was more like, you know – there's some companies like they do make, you know, arty sort of things and textiles and that sort of thing. So I've tried to look at those more and the other things did put me off.

Interviewer:	Do you think that university could help you more in finding the placements?

Subject:	Yeah, I think they could – yeah, I think they could because you know, I think something could be done to make it, you know, make you not feel quite so - it's quite daunting like, you think oh well, you either go on one or you don't but if you're going on one and you have to look through – you search on the internet for all these placements, that are obviously on the careers site – but there are only so many, so you have to go further afield from that, and I don't actually know where to look really. I've tried to type stuff in on – you know, the internet, but I've just not really come up with anything.

Interviewer:	OK, what are you most looking forward to and most worried about going on placement?

Subject:	Er, l think looking forward to well, getting a break from the course. I think that when you come back then in the final year, then it'll be a much sort of fresher perspective and you'll have like some more skills and you'll have thought – you know, you won't be like – still at this early – you'll probably feel a bit older because you've had, you know, more in experience. Erm, the worst thing is probably to, the whole– a whole different year, environment, I think and the work – you just don't know what to expect or anything.

Interviewer:	OK, how do you think work will be different from university?

Subject:	Er, I think it will be much – it probably you know, you've got to like keep to deadlines and things and I think it'll probably – I think it'll probably encourage you more to do the work because it's a part of the company, you know, everyone's in it and you've got to get it done otherwise you'll let the team down. Whereas, obviously, with deadlines, you know, on the course, you're going to say oh of course, that doesn't matter, you forget about it for now, I don't want to think about it, I don't want to do it, whereas I think that in the workplace it'd be good because people may – you know, will help you probably, you know, if you're a bit stuck and then say, oh we'll do it like this or. Which is sometimes what you need.

Interviewer:	OK, in terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in say 5 years time?

Subject:	Erm, I think I'll probably be doing something totally different from the course. I think I'll probably – or maybe something quite related. Obviously – I'm quite – I like in the first year we did ergonomics, you know, and I would maybe – the sort of careers things that I can see myself in, they'd either be something like that or sustainable design – you know working in a team, you know brainstorming different ideas for products and stuff, or something like more – much more arty or I would – I could see myself sort of doing more textiles sort of thing, because I really enjoy that making – coming up with designs for clothes and like accessories and stuff, so maybe something like that. I'm not sure.

Interviewer:	OK, what about in 10 years time?

Subject:	Oh God.

Interviewer:	Would you like to go into managing people, or would you like to perhaps just become more specialised?

Subject:	Yeah, I think it would be good – yeah, it would be good to be more specialised. You'd be part of like really an established sort of company, and you know, just be really secure in that and you know, have a good time as well as you know, producing good work and stuff.

Interviewer:	So what would be an ideal career?

Subject:	I think my ideal career would be – I want to be quite high up. I'd like to work for like a group of like people, like your small group, brainstorming ideas and coming up with you know, I'd like to do something different every day really, like one day doing, thinking about things and then another day you'll be going out investigating. Or I do sort of quite like the researching sort of aspects as well. They're just like constantly different every day and yet have a team where you all group your ideas together and then you'll find that you can bounce like ideas off each other – it's much easier that way. And stuff that you haven't thought – you're like oh right, I never thought of that like – it's really good I think.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that you'll come across any difficulties trying to get or achieve that?

Subject:	Yeah, I think it will be really difficult because with these – with that sort, you know, sort of field it is very difficult to get jobs. Whereas, with things – I'd say more – the things that people think are more academic – say English, Maths and Physics, they are much easier to get jobs, whereas with erm courses like this, you know, I think it will be very difficult. I do worry that, you know, I won't be able to get a job at the end sort of thing.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the career prospects are …

Subject:	Yeah, I think it will be very difficult to get a job but I'm thinking that if I can't get anything that I really enjoy – you know – through that – then, 'cos I do quite like a lot of broad things, so it would be a bit easier, then I think I'll probably teach – if I can't you know, find anything else, 'cos I think I'd really enjoy that.

Interviewer:	OK, that's good.

Subject:	Because obviously then, I'd know the problems I'd had and then I could apply that and then say oh, I think you know – we can just, you know. 'Cos you've had experience it would be much easier then to tell – you know, pass on to them, so…

Interviewer:	OK, are you happy with all the career choices that you've made so far, would you do it all again?

Subject:	I think I am. I think – obviously I do – when I got here, I was supposed to be in the first year and sometimes now I do think, oh, is this degree actually going to get me anywhere? And should I have took something more academic? And should I have like – sometimes I think I should have maybe took something more arty 'cos – like graphic design, 'cos one of my housemates does do that, and the projects she has are more like really and I think oh wow, that's really cool. (Lost words). Yeah, with my course, sometimes a lot of the aspects I'm not that keen on but then I think, at the end of the day, with a course like this – like people have said that, 'cos it's so broad and it's – you can like [university's] a well-established university and everyone wants graduates from [this university], then it probably will – you know – get me – you'll be able to get your foot in the door and then use a lot of skills like (?) or something, be able to apply those. 

Interviewer:	Overall, have you enjoyed the course?

Subject:	Yeah, I probably would say. Well, obviously some aspects I hate but there is – you know there is some that I do like. It's hard to say, I change from day to day.

Interviewer:	OK, what 5 words would you apply to like the culture or the characteristics of design and technology industry?

Subject:	I'd probably say creative, erm, (long pause) I have to think about it – I'd probably say creative, technical, broad, mm, it's so difficult.

Interviewer:	Would you say it's masculine?

Subject:	I think at school I always thought it's more feminine because obviously we had the choices you either did design and technology, then you did all of your systems or there was resistant materials. So, I always felt the guys generally went for resistant materials whereas all the girls usually go for design and technology. And at school it was more – you know – creative. It was more girly – you didn't make all the stuff. Whereas when I got to this here, it does seem more masculine because you do make a lot and in a workshop like machining and stuff like that and I hated that part of it as well. I was surprised that I had to do all that sort of thing, because at secondary school we never did anything with machinery and when I got here it was like, oh well today we're gonna do some lazering and I want you to do this. And I was like oh my God, I've never done this before and I had to like, obviously ask a lot and my finished thing, I wasn't that happy with it because I just – you know – it was very experimental oh they think that I'm (?) That's why it was so difficult. So I think it would be a little bit – at secondary school, if I'd been prepared for it more, maybe had more of that on the curriculum, whereas you know, at my school and college we didn't really have that, whereas I know some other people, at their college and stuff, they did do all that sort of thing, so then when they came here it was much easier for them, so I did find that really difficult and I felt like Oh God, it's like starting primary school again.

Interviewer:	Were you surprised by how many girls were on the course?

Subject:	No, I did sort of think there would be more males actually than females, with it being industrial design technology I thought there would be more males on the course, yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think it will stay like that?

Subject:	I think it's grad – I think it is increasing, the number of females. I'm sure like every year it does go up, because I mean – a few years ago there would have been just all males but now I think – I think maybe females are, you know, beginning to think, you know, oh if they can do it, we can do it, so.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that anything about the culture will cause you any problems? Or like the fact that it is masculine …?

Subject:	Yeah, sometimes it does – you do feel a bit like inadequate sometimes. You think oh well, oh I find that really difficult but then like why can they do it really easy? Or how can they get their brains out and when mines just like, not taking it in? So yeah, I do find that sometimes yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, that's it then really. Thank you.

Subject:	That's OK.

Interviewer:	Thank you for your help.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I'll tell you a bit about what I'm doing – we're looking at women students, mainly engineering students. We're also doing the work in another university, and the design and technology side comes under engineering there, so we've included it here as well. The main thing we're looking at is the fact that engineering's male dominated, so it will be interesting to get your views on that side of thing as well. So we're really trying to improve the situation for women in engineering. Erm, are you going on a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I'm not sure, I've applied to [company] so far and some others I've looked at, but erm, I'm actually living in [university town] next year, so whatever I get, you know, I want to be in travelling distance – so I'm going to apply for a few places, but if not, then I'll just carry on to the third year.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: We'll start off with a few background questions about why you chose the course. OK, what is the course exactly?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Industrial design and technology.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What A levels did you do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I did Art, English Literature, Design and Technology and then I did general studies. I also did an AS in Biology, but dropped that – it wasn't really for me.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What type of school did you go to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, just a normal, basic school.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes, not an all girls school or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh no.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Erm, have you got any previous work experience in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, no none at all, no.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, what do your parents do – are either of them engineers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: My dad's an engineer – well, that's what course he did – he's a Project Manager, and my mum just works part time.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, when and why then do you think that you decided to do design and technology?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, I'd already been interested – well through school, I'd always been interested in Art and I'd always wanted to do something with that and then I got to college and I did design and technology and I did really enjoy that as well and I thought doing the technology will be using my brain more than the arts – you know people always say oh I can't get a job in a art, so I thought oh, I'll take that course then. And I do still enjoy you know, some arty aspects, and I do try and get – you know – sort of that into my work. Yeah, I decided – I was either going to be a graphic designer or it was just, you know, design technology and talking to my tutors and everything and they said, oh well maybe you should go for the design technology then it's a bit – it's not – it's still a bit creative but you can use your brain in other aspects of the stuff rather than going for a tot – you know graphic design – it's hard to get a job in those sort of areas. So then I decided on industrial design in the end. I didn't quite realise how much technology would be involved though, 'cos like on the open day they said – I said, oh well I did Maths at GCSE, and I got an A for that, and so will I be OK? And they said, oh yeah, if you get the C at GCSE you're fine and I got here and it was really difficult, I found it really hard. And a lot of people did. I think a few of the people did drop out in the first year because, it didn't seem to be specified that – you know actually that you'd be having electronics every week and then you swap over and do mechanics and you'll have tests on these and then. Yeah, I did Ok on some of the mechanics stuff, 'cos I didn't – well, they teach you, you know – taught that quite well, but some of the electronics I did really struggle on that, so it did sort of put me off the course but then I thought I'll stick with it and see, you know, if it gets easier and obviously this year I didn't have to take that – I chose, you know, other aspects that I preferred so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you have much advice and that, from careers advisors, then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I didn't really at secondary school. I didn't really – they never said that much, to be honest, but I sort of always had in my mind, that I knew which sort of course I wanted to do and so it was just a matter of deciding whether it was going to be graphics or design technology, so, you know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did your family influence your decision at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, they did sort of because my Mum did say well, maybe you should do industrial design, instead of graphic design because it's – you know – quite difficult to get a job in graphics design. Yet with something like industrial design, because there's a lot of different areas you can go into then, they said you're probably better to do that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you think about doing the sandwich course when you applied for the course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, when I applied for the course they said oh, you can put down the sandwich course anyway, even if you decide not to do it. So I thought well I'll put down for it, because you know, a lot of people say that obviously it'll help you in your job if you've had some work experience, because nowadays that's what they look for. Rather than oh, you've got this grade, or whatever, it's what experience you've got so I thought it'd be valuable to put that down…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how did you decide to come to [this university]?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well that was – I put down – I had loads of universities and I thought, oh I don't know which one to go to, went all over the country like going to student days there, just thought seeing like the feel about the place, what I preferred and it came down to either [university] or here and – because my tutor said, oh, have you looked at [this university]? 'Cos I hadn't – I'd never really heard of it and he said, oh 'cos it's really good for design and technology and everything. So I came here and I thought, oh yeah, it does seem really good and it's like an academic sort of university and everything. So I thought oh yeah – I decided to come here in the end. But I was very umming and ahhing like till the last minute.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, is design and technology very male dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, yeah, there isn't very many females on the course. Obviously its increasing all the time but I do find that, obviously, in the first year, with all the electronics and mechanics, there's – the guys can think it – you know, with different parts of their brain to like –apply it to that sort of thing whereas I think – some girls are really good at it as well – you know – it's quite, you know, a hard thing to get it – you know – to take that on board.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What characteristics do you think make a good designer and do you think any of those characteristics are more male or female?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I suppose the – well there is like an Arty sort of side, you know, the sort of creative side, which is a lot of – erm, it did surprise me actually, because a lot of the males are very good at that as well, whereas at secondary school it's always been more the female sort of side, whereas men do more – do making and things. And also, we have projects where we had to make like prototypes – just models and stuff – and I found that quite difficult because I'd never done it before, whereas the boys, they, even though they've not done as much they seem to have like a better understanding of how to do it. Like, they got told, then they could apply it straight away – whereas I had to ask them again and again how to do it – I just couldn't get my head around them.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that more women should be encouraged to do design and technology?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think it is good that you know – to encourage more people to do it, if it's – well, it's a good course, you know, and very varied so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why do you think that more women don't do it – do you think that's because they don't know what it is?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, maybe. I'd have thought, because I applied to like loads of different places for like design and technology and then, here, it was the industrial design, but I sort of thought that was the same as design and technology, so I looked at it, you know, and looked at loads of different universities and I realise now that the industrial design is obviously more technical than say the course at [university] which was design technology. So yeah, I suppose people don't really understand it totally and I can't remember in the prospectus, whether it actually said I would be doing electronics and mechanics. I think all I thought as well would be oh you'd be doing like ergonomics, and sizes and – which I did really enjoy that part and then, obviously, aesthetics and everything. I didn't know if it said – you know – about those or not.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think could be done to let people know more about it. Do you think that's down to – purely down to school or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it's probably – yeah, through careers advice or you know, because I'm sure people kind of think oh, I won't be able to do that, because it's got this in it or its all male dominated, but I think sort of now, it does seem to be – more people do seem to be interested in doing these, you know, all these sort of careers. I think it's like – because in hall last year, we had a few engineering students and some of those were girls and they did seem to get on OK on the course and obviously you think sometimes oh that's quite odd that they're doing it but, so, my dad did – because he'd worked in engineering, he said that they're always looking for like – now – they've got like 1 female engineer and he said that she's really thorough, because obviously, it depends whether - the guys tend to be 'oh yeah, I'll just do it like that' or whether there's quite – he said that she's really good, so. I suppose they should be encouraged to say oh look, you can do it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there are any advantages to being a woman in a male dominated …?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think so because er – especially when we've done like er group work or things like that. We have different perspectives than the males. I think also – I also, personally, I try to see things a bit differently as well, because I enjoy not the technical side, I'll look into more arty stuff and there are different ways to do stuff. And I think it is much more interesting having, like a broad range of people, come up with such different ideas.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there are disadvantages?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I suppose a disadvantage – er, I feel that I'm not quite as technology er minded as some of the guys are.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, I'm going to ask you a few questions about the course and that now. You've said a bit about the course not being exactly what you expected it to be (yeah) but what do you think have been the best and the worst things about the course so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, the best thing is – I enjoy working within – I do quite like working in the group work like, I very much like brain storming, you know, at the beginning of a project and stuff like in a small group or er we've done presentations and things as well. At first I thought, oh no, I hate doing them but it does get you much more used to it, ready for – say in design – we had part of that, the assessment was to do presentations – so that was really good. And then, also erm just sort of other presentation boards and sketching's quite good. I don't always like it when you have to – say when the specification – like's so rigid, and they say do this and you have like, you know, follow it totally. I like it when – like we've recently had this project on – it was researching into different topics for (?) and I had waking up and going to sleep. It's also about – really interesting like asking people all what do you like? What do you hate? And taking like – recording it and photos as well and then we created a board to do that. Like you can see that obviously all the different presentation boards were totally different, because obviously how things are perceived is different. But I did really enjoy doing that because you can put much more of your influence into it rather than saying oh, do a ¾ perspective of this product. There are also things that I don't like, sort of electronics. I'm not keen on the CAD – you know – computer aided design. I just find it really difficult. I just – to get my head round it, I just like – I think it makes it a challenge – I haven't done it before and – I mean I do – I can do stuff – you know some stuff now, which I couldn't do before but I still struggle a bit and initially – when I get an assignment of it, I'm like oh no.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think then, like you said you like doing the group work and presentations and stuff – do you think that'll help you when you go to work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, definitely, yeah. I think the group work's really good, so erm, understand like how to deal with anyone that thinks differently and yet trying to get all that group together to come up with a solution and things. And, obviously, the presentations erm although sometimes you might dread them, they are really useful because you'll have to do that anyway, whatever job you go into really. So it's confidence and things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When you do group work, how do you decide who to work with, in your groups?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, sometimes we get set them, which is quite good I suppose, because then you can have a mix of different people you haven't worked with and you can get to know other people – what they think about. Or, recently, at the moment, we're just in a group and we pick that ourselves, so usually just friends or whatever. I don't usually go for like well, I'll go with them, they're really good at things. I just usually go with friends and then I know that we'll get on and we'll be able to motivate each other and such like.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you prefer to work with men or women or doesn't it bother you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I don't mind to be honest – either. I think it's good to have a mixture, really. And on our course you always do because there's hardly any females – there all dotted about, but there's more – you know – more males.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you had any really bad experiences with group work at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I haven't really, to be honest. I know sometimes it's hard – like, if there's one person who's not pulling their weight, but I've never really had that, so it's been OK, you know so far.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Out of interest, what are the gender proportions?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think there are probably about – I'm trying to think how many females there are. Maybe about – I'd say maybe about a quarter female and the rest male. Something about that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that the same with lecturers as well – do you have any female lecturers at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, the only – we used to have – well, we had – one of our Heads of year, she was called [name], but she left and we had a – but mostly they're all males, to be honest. I don't think they have any – we have one lady actually for sustainable, but yeah, they're generally male, you know for the CAD and then – I think it would be quite good having a female actually, teaching from a (?) then you probably get a better perspective on it, because obviously the males are like – they explain it in a different way, which is sometimes hard to follow.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it would be quite encouraging having a female?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it would, yeah, because then you'd think oh well, look how well they're doing – I'll try and you know, apply for that. Yeah, I never thought about that before but I think that would be quite good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the male lecturers treat the female and male students the same?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er I think sometimes they make like – I find that sometimes, within technology sort of thing, you'll ask them a question and they'll tell you, then you still haven't got it and then they sort of think – 'what do you mean, you don't understand?' And sometimes I think you don't get – they don't think it'll help. But then, if you say, oh we're only here to lecture, we're not here to teach, but it is quite difficult when you do ask, they sort of explain it and then you're like well, I still don't get that. And I often have to ask males in the group and then they'll explain it and I'm like, oh right, that's what he's going on about, I know now - so yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you got a personal tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are they male or female?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Male, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you rather have a female for your tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think there's one – I think there's one lady – female – I think all the rest are male, so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you rather have a female?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think it would be good, actually, to have a female, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think they'd be more approachable?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I do find that our tutors aren't very approachable and I find with [name] – well she's very approachable, you can ask her about anything, I'd feel comfortable asking her, you know, about your problems or anything, but I do find some of the others like – I wouldn't ever want to go and say, oh, what do you mean about this but I feel like they think I'm stupid or oh what do you mean do you didn't know it? Because I do often get that impression so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that that's a bit as well, because you are a woman?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, it could be maybe yeah, although some like – we do have someone in for electronics and he's male and obviously he helps the females more and so the guys get annoyed about that and he's alright to help you. He's like oh let me help you with that circuit and then the guys will come up to him and ask him and he's like oh well, oh you do it like this but then sends them all off – so that's quite good – using it to your advantage.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What bits of the teaching and advice that you've had might help you when you get on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don't really think – feel that anything would, to be honest. I don't – I mean the teaching it's more – I think you have to do it more off your own back, to be honest, because you – as we said – they just lecture, they don't really – they're not bothered about if you – really, you know, you can understand it really, because they're just there to tell you about all the facts and then you have to apply it yourself and advice I haven't really – I meant I don't ever really go and talk to my personal tutor because I don't find that, you know, it'd be that beneficial really. So…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there are any skills that you've learnt, on the course, that will help you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, I think, well I've gained more confidence, obviously through the group work and getting on with other people, and presentations. I mean I must say – you could say like working to deadlines, but I still leave things to the last minute – I always plan to do them, you know, but it never happens. And I've been finding a lot of people on the course are – do seem very organised and I wish they could like, you know, rub some of that off onto me. I could do with some of that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you feel ready to go on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I don't, no. And I think that's why I sort of, you know, holding back a bit not totally – like a lot of people that have applied to all them places and have got – some people have got accepted already. But I sort of – you know, left it till the last minute. I've applied to [company] but I looked at some others on the internet but I'm just sort of like thinking, oh God, I don't think I can do these things, like it looks very like you've got to be efficient in CAD and stuff and I'm like well, I'm not really that, you know. I don't feel that I could be you know, be out in the workplace, if someone was telling me to do something, I'd be like, oh God, you know. But also, I've looked at some placements which are quite different, so I do like – in my freetime, I like making like bags and clothes and stuff, so I've sort of looked into some stuff like that. So I might apply to some of those – like more craft sort of things rather than in technology sort of things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the university could do more to help prepare you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think there would be a lot – it's like just to help you get – I mean we had help with CVs and you know, how to approach – your work and stuff together, but yeah it would be handy to like have something, even if it's partly like the tutors would say, you know, we're going to have a meeting with every one of you and talk to you about how – you know – and what you want to do and stuff – I think that would be quite useful.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you had the chance to speak to anyone like that's been on the course before and maybe been on a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, that'd be quite useful, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think will be the good things about going on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, money (laughs). It'll be good to like, because obviously – I don't think the company that I plan to work for (?). I think it will be good to like have a different sort of outlook on the course, 'cos I do find like and I do often go through stages and I'm like Oh God, I'm not sure if I'm on the right course. I should have done like English or something – because, you know, to have more time for fun stuff rather than like always – 'cos this course is like really demanding and it's always – you're always thinking about it, you've always got a deadline, and it just seems like really stressful whereas, in my house, like there's other people who are doing like other courses and who don't have much to do, yet they'll get better grades at the end of the day.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it's seems strange that you're in the social sciences and humanities faculty?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, it does seem quite odd, yeah, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When you've been looking at the companies –have you been looking at the type of work that you'll be doing or have you been looking at things like training opportunities and the pay and things like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, just sort of looking at the – what you'd have to do really, and what sort of skills they want so you know, I can see whether I'd be suitable for it or not. Because, obviously they're not that detailed in, you know, the description – I mean you might be OK, some of the work so they do obviously get – it's the way they've worded it, you're like Oh no, I wouldn't be able to do any of that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you done much research on the different companies then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I just – well the only place I've looked is on the –you know – [university] – careers website – I've just looked at industrial placements on there. But a lot are very technical which I obviously don't want, so I sort of looked in the – like you can go on the database and I was like crafts for – and it was more like, you know – there's some companies like they do make, you know, arty sort of things and textiles and that sort of thing. So I've tried to look at those more and the other things did put me off.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that university could help you more in finding the placements?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think they could – yeah, I think they could because you know, I think something could be done to make it, you know, make you not feel quite so - it's quite daunting like, you think oh well, you either go on one or you don't but if you're going on one and you have to look through – you search on the internet for all these placements, that are obviously on the careers site – but there are only so many, so you have to go further afield from that, and I don't actually know where to look really. I've tried to type stuff in on – you know, the internet, but I've just not really come up with anything.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what are you most looking forward to and most worried about going on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, l think looking forward to well, getting a break from the course. I think that when you come back then in the final year, then it'll be a much sort of fresher perspective and you'll have like some more skills and you'll have thought – you know, you won't be like – still at this early – you'll probably feel a bit older because you've had, you know, more in experience. Erm, the worst thing is probably to, the whole– a whole different year, environment, I think and the work – you just don't know what to expect or anything.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how do you think work will be different from university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I think it will be much – it probably you know, you've got to like keep to deadlines and things and I think it'll probably – I think it'll probably encourage you more to do the work because it's a part of the company, you know, everyone's in it and you've got to get it done otherwise you'll let the team down. Whereas, obviously, with deadlines, you know, on the course, you're going to say oh of course, that doesn't matter, you forget about it for now, I don't want to think about it, I don't want to do it, whereas I think that in the workplace it'd be good because people may – you know, will help you probably, you know, if you're a bit stuck and then say, oh we'll do it like this or. Which is sometimes what you need.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, in terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in say 5 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think I'll probably be doing something totally different from the course. I think I'll probably – or maybe something quite related. Obviously – I'm quite – I like in the first year we did ergonomics, you know, and I would maybe – the sort of careers things that I can see myself in, they'd either be something like that or sustainable design – you know working in a team, you know brainstorming different ideas for products and stuff, or something like more – much more arty or I would – I could see myself sort of doing more textiles sort of thing, because I really enjoy that making – coming up with designs for clothes and like accessories and stuff, so maybe something like that. I'm not sure.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what about in 10 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh God.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you like to go into managing people, or would you like to perhaps just become more specialised?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think it would be good – yeah, it would be good to be more specialised. You'd be part of like really an established sort of company, and you know, just be really secure in that and you know, have a good time as well as you know, producing good work and stuff.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So what would be an ideal career?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think my ideal career would be – I want to be quite high up. I'd like to work for like a group of like people, like your small group, brainstorming ideas and coming up with you know, I'd like to do something different every day really, like one day doing, thinking about things and then another day you'll be going out investigating. Or I do sort of quite like the researching sort of aspects as well. They're just like constantly different every day and yet have a team where you all group your ideas together and then you'll find that you can bounce like ideas off each other – it's much easier that way. And stuff that you haven't thought – you're like oh right, I never thought of that like – it's really good I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that you'll come across any difficulties trying to get or achieve that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think it will be really difficult because with these – with that sort, you know, sort of field it is very difficult to get jobs.
